newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: OPPOSITION MARCHES IN KABILA'S CONGO DESPITE BAN.
newsitem.headline: OPPOSITION MARCHES IN KABILA'S CONGO DESPITE BAN.

text.p: Several hundred opposition supporters marched in Kinshasa, the capital of Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of Congo, on Wednesday in defiance of a ban on demonstrations and political activity.

Earlier, soldiers from Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL) sealed off a nearby campus, dispersed hundreds of chanting students there and prevented them joining the march.

Kabila himself, who will be inaugurated as head of state in the capital on Thursday, left the city on Tuesday for the southern mining capital of Lubumbashi. Officials declined to say why but added they expected him back later on Wednesday.

Students fleeing soldiers at the Higher of Institute of Commerce, a hotbed of opposition to ousted dictator Mobutu Sese Sseko, denounced the presence of Rwandans among Kabila's forces and said all foreign troops must return home.
"Kabila should have a chance but we do not want the Rwandans," one student told Reuters. "We just do not want the Rwandans. They have got to go."
A couple of hundred chanting supporters of veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi later set off for the city centre from the capital's central railway station, the rallying point for the march.
Soldiers initially barred their route. The march swelled to several hundred protesters after the soldiers stepped back and allowed them to continue down the main June 30 Boulevard.
Dozens of soldiers, who arrived in trucks, sealed off the campus, preventing students leaving for the railway station.
"We are here to bring order, that is all," their commander told Reuters. He declined to give his name.
Kabila's Alliance, which entered Kinshasa on May 17 and toppled Mobutu after a seven-month civil war, has banned political activity and public demonstrations.
Tshisekedi's Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) has called marches for Wednesday and Friday.

"We are marching to protest about the Rwandans," said Jean- Claude Mukendi, an unemployed youth and supporter of Tshisekedi, a longstanding Mobutu opponent. "Mr Tshisekedi knows the Zairean people do not want to be ruled by foreigners."
Jean-Marie Vianney Kabukanye, national secretary of the youth wing of the UDPS, told Reuters on the eve of the march that the opposition rejected Kabila's policies.
"We have not changed Mobutu to replace him with another Mobutu. The man has changed but not the policies," he said.
"Foreign troops must leave as soon as possible or risk appearing like occupation troops," Vianney said.
Tshisekedi, citing a 1992 vote in a sovereign national conference in what was then Zaire, has doggedly insisted over the years that constitutionally he is prime minister.
Opposition activists say he should be allowed to take office as such.
Kabila has set up a 13-member government. Aides say he plans to name seven more ministers but not a prime minister.
Kinshasa newspapers dished up a mixed bag of headlines with the independent Reference Plus predicting a showdown between Tshisekedi's party and Kabila's Alliance on Wednesday.

Palmares, close to the opposition, headlined U.S. pressure on Kabila to broaden his government. Le Soft, whose proprietor was Mobutu's last information minister, spoke of a "totalitariatian lurch" under Kabila.
Opposition activists marched in Kinshasa on Friday and Saturday. Kabila forces fired in the air and took away some protesters. Government officials said they were later released.
